Source and attribution

The archive attributes this English wording to Parerga und Paralipomena (on compassion) and files it under Voluntarism. That locator distinguishes the passage from loose internet attributions: readers can return to the named work or section to check translation, surrounding argument, and edition-specific wording.

About Arthur Schopenhauer

Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) was a German philosopher of pessimism whose The World as Will and Representation fused Kantian phenomena with a blind metaphysical will. Largely ignored while Hegel dominated Berlin, he later won fame influencing artists and psychologists.

How to read this passage

Greek distinctions among eros, philia, and agape, Confucian relational ethics, and modern debates about romantic love keep the theme philosophically precise rather than merely sentimental. This passage enters that discussion through love, morality, otherness.

Concepts in this quote

Love
Love in philosophy ranges from friendship and desire to care, justice, and the transformation of the self.
Morality
Morality in philosophy concerns right and wrong, obligation, and the standards by which we judge persons and acts.
Otherness
Otherness appears in this archive as a live philosophical concern—not a slogan. These verified English passages show how thinkers treat otherness as a problem of judgment, practice, or explanation.
